title: Multi-maturity consistency of option prices under bounded bid-ask spreads: a minimal obstruction and an exact two-date basket operator

p.t: Finite option quotes encode a geometric no-arbitrage problem. In a frictionless one-period market, monotonicity, convexity, and the slope bounds of the call-price curve lead to explicit consistency conditions (Carr and Madan, 2005;Davis and Hobson, 2007;Cousot, 2007). With several maturities, convex order supplies the intertemporal restriction. Bid-ask spreads make both parts subtler: long and short static positions execute at different prices, and dynamic stock trades cross a spread whose orientation is observed only when the trade is made. Gerhold and Gülüm (2020) study a particularly sharp version of this problem. Calls are cash settled against a nontraded reference price S C , while a shadow martingale S * must remain inside the bid-ask spread of the dynamically traded stock. The discounted spread has a deterministic absolute width bound ϵ. Their one-maturity conditions are complete. For several maturities they introduce calendar-vertical baskets (CVBs) and derive four families of necessary inequalities. Conjecture 5.4 of Gerhold and Gülüm (2020) has two parts: it asks whether those four families are also sufficient for consistency, and it predicts weak arbitrage when the first three hold but the strict fourth condition fails. A sign inconsistency in the cited CVB bid must first be resolved. The contract contains a cash term -2ϵ1 {σ 1 =-1} , while the displayed bid in Gerhold and Gülüm (2020, Definition 5.1 and equation ( 22)) adds 2ϵ on that face. The contract, the paper's self-financing convention, and the liquidation calculation in its Lemma 5.2 instead give an executable bid with a minus sign. The distinction is substantive: the printed bid can violate a claimed necessary inequality in a constant, perfectly consistent model. We therefore study the corrected executable question: after replacing the sign and adjoining the initial and complete one-maturity requirements, are the resulting conditions sufficient?

The answer is no at the smallest possible multi-date quote complexity. The economic obstruction is a stock flip. Shorting an earlier call and buying a fractional later call allows a trader to hold no stock after a low first-date state and a short stock position after a high state. A single CVB comparison does not encode this coupled switch. Theorem 1.1 (Main result). For every ϵ > 0, there is a two-date panel with one actual call quote at each date such that: (i) the initial spread and the complete one-maturity consistency conditions hold; (ii) all corrected executable CVB conditions hold, strictly whenever the source requires a strict face; (iii) the strategy consisting of 2/3 of a share, one short date-one call, and 1/3 of a long date-two call has setup cost -47 150 ϵ and nonnegative liquidation on every admissible path; (iv) this counterexample persists on a six-dimensional open box of quote panels. Two quoted dates and two actual calls, necessarily split one per date, are minimal for such an augmented intertemporal counterexample. Moreover, for every payoff h 2 generated by a finite terminal call portfolio, every initial stock holding θ, and x ≥ ϵ, the two-date continuation operator is the following. p.s: Together with the date-one static payoff, this operator characterizes the full two-date finite-call model-independent-arbitrage basket cone.
p.t: The finite-panel assertions and minimality are proved in Theorem 3.2, the open-box statement in Theorem 3.4, and the operator assertions in Theorem 5.2 and Theorem 5.4. The counterexample is not isolated. The six quote coordinates may be perturbed independently while preserving every tested condition and the negative setup cost. Nor is its certificate tied to the trading strategy: the extremal call-function envelopes from Gerhold and Gülüm (2019) force a convex-order gap of 47ϵ/50; after multiplication by the terminal call weight 1/3, this equals the initial gain 47ϵ/150. Relation to prior work. Consistent price systems and fundamental theorems under transaction costs have a long history (Jouini and Kallal, 1995;Schachermayer, 2004;Pennanen and Penner, 2010;Bouchard and Nutz, 2016;Bayraktar and Zhang, 2016). Probability-free and robust superhedging recursions under frictions appear in Dolinsky and Soner (2014) and Burzoni (2016). Cheridito et al. (2017) allow state-dependent convex dynamic costs and finite static portfolios in arbitrary derivatives, a framework that contains the present execution architecture after a direct encoding. Specializing that architecture to the bounded reference/shadow spread yields the penalty -ϵ(|q -θ| + |q|), the scalar convex-envelope formula, and a finite evaluation rule. An explicit restricted-support convex-envelope recursion also appears in Chapter 5 of Bauer (2024). Adjacent finite-quote work uses different market assumptions. Cohen et al. (2020) treat static repair with a frictionless underlying. Computational martingale optimal transport fixes marginal laws and relaxes martingale constraints for numerical purposes (Guo and Obłój, 2019). The current bid-ask martingale optimal transport duality of Liang et al. (2026) allows vanilla bid-ask execution but keeps dynamic trading in the underlying frictionless. None of these formulations contains simultaneously the absolute stock-spread bound, the distinct reference and shadow prices, and the finite execution structure studied here.

Section 2 gives a self-contained discounted market and separates the printed and executable CVB systems. Section 3 proves the stock-flip bridge, the counterexample family for every ϵ > 0, and its open neighborhood. Section 4 gives the independent convex-order certificate. Section 5 derives the two-date operator, including the compact minimax reduction, conjugate representation, attainment, and Borel selector. Section 6 shows that adding every pairwise stock-flip bridge still does not close the full basket cone, and records the scope of the results.

The sign issue can be seen directly from the contract. In the notation of Gerhold and Gülüm (2020, Definition 5.1), a CVB of maturity u < T has cash settlement The indices and signs obey the path-matching restrictions in that definition; their details are immaterial for the accounting identity. Proposition 2.1 (Printed versus executable bid). The amount received by selling CVB u , before following the dynamic liquidation rule, is The +2ϵ adjustment in the printed CVB bid is inconsistent with (4), the executable option accounting, and the self-financing identity. Proof. Selling (4) reverses every static position. Its date-zero cost, using option bids for shorts and asks for longs, is This is the negative of ( 5). It is also the initial-value identity asserted in the source's Lemma 5.2. The dynamic stock calculation in that proof is consistent with this expression. The distinction changes necessity, not merely notation. Example 2.2 (A consistent constant model violating the printed necessary condition). Take ϵ = 1, a constant reference and shadow price equal to 5, zero stock spread, and a strike-2 call worth 3 at both dates. This is a consistent model. For the face σ 1 = -1, however, the printed formula assigns the earlier CVB the bid 3 + 2 = 5 at shifted strike 2 + 1 = 3. The later shifted ask at the same point is 3, so the printed monotonicity condition would require 5 ≤ 3. The executable bid is instead 3 -2 = 1, as required by the contract.

The same sign pattern appears in Gülüm (2016, Definition 3.10, equation (3.20), and Proposition 3.11), in arXiv:1608.05585v1 and v2, and in the published article of Gerhold and Gülüm (2020). In each case the contract and self-financing calculation use -2ϵ, while the displayed bid uses +2ϵ. This is an algebraic comparison of the formulas, not an attribution of authorial intent. Accordingly, the result below has two separate implications. The literally printed system is not necessary. After replacing its bid by (5), necessity survives, but even the base-augmented executable system is not sufficient.

Corollary 3.4 (Open quote box). Fix ϵ > 0 and the strikes 3ϵ and 5ϵ. Perturb each of the six bid and ask coordinates in (16)-( 17) independently by less than ϵ/200. Every resulting quote panel remains a base-augmented executable-CVB counterexample with stock-flip arbitrage. Proof. Every bid-ask width remains between ϵ/100 and 3ϵ/100; in particular, the initial width remains below ϵ. The call values 5ϵ and 2ϵ, and the common shadow mean 6ϵ, remain inside their respective perturbed quote intervals, so the one-maturity witnesses in the proof of Theorem 3.2 still apply. The slack in each non-strict CVB inequality changes by less than ϵ/100: its variable part is one bid coordinate subtracted from one ask coordinate or a convex combination of two ask coordinates. Remark 3.5 (Status of Conjecture 5.4). Once bid execution is made explicit, the source statement separates into three claims. Theorem 5.2 is a complete characterization of the model-independent-arbitrage cone. It is not by itself a characterization of the probabilistic consistency set (2). Consistency always rules out modelindependent arbitrage, but the converse can fail on weak-arbitrage boundaries. This distinction already occurs in the source's one-maturity theorem when its equality condition fails: under every candidate model, some model-dependent arbitrage exists, yet there is no single pathwise strategy that is strict on all possible models. The strict counterexample in Theorem 3.2 lies away from this boundary and is unaffected by the distinction. A complete identification of the operator cone with consistency on the remaining equality faces would require an additional closure or density theorem.

The counterexample concerns the corrected, base-augmented executable CVB system; the distinct weak-arbitrage clause of Conjecture 5.4 remains open. The minimality statement counts quoted dates and actual call quotes in the finite-call framework of Gerhold and Gülüm. The operator is complete for two-date finite-call baskets as the static coefficients range over R, but it does not provide a finite irredundant representation of that cone. Extensions to three or more dates and the frictionless limit ϵ = 0 are beyond the present scope.

Correcting the CVB bid does not repair the multi-maturity sufficiency problem. The corrected executable system fails for every positive spread bound at the first possible intertemporal quote complexity: two dates and one actual call at each. The stock flip gives both a transparent executable arbitrage and a matching convex-order separation, and the failure is stable on an open set of quotes. The backward operator shows why no small list of single transported calls should be expected to capture the whole pathwise geometry. It first convexifies the terminal static payoff and then searches a 2ϵ-neighborhood generated by the two adverse spread crossings, with an additional one-sided term from the initial stock. The minimal stock flip is the smallest visible instance of that broader basket geometry.
